presentingComplaint: Abnormal pre-operative full blood count with unexplained pancytopenia and spontaneous bruising in an elderly man admitted for elective total knee replacement.
history: A 74-year-old retired schoolteacher was admitted electively for a right total knee replacement. He is on chronic polypharmacy: warfarin for permanent atrial fibrillation (target INR 2-3), metformin and gliclazide for type 2 diabetes, amlodipine and ramipril for hypertension, atorvastatin, omeprazole, and allopurinol for gout. Over the preceding 5-6 weeks he had noticed progressive fatigue and breathlessness on climbing stairs, easy bruising over both forearms, occasional gum bleeding when brushing, drenching night sweats, and about 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. The bruising had initially been attributed to his warfarin by his GP, and a dose reduction had been advised. Routine pre-operative bloods were markedly abnormal, prompting cancellation of surgery and a haematology referral. No fevers with rigors, no localising infective symptoms, no recent antibiotics or hospitalisation, no NSAID or new drug exposure. No prior chemotherapy or radiation; no known haematological disorder.
examination: Elderly man, comfortable at rest but pale. Widespread ecchymoses over both forearms and shins with scattered petechiae on the lower legs and buccal mucosa; a small amount of dried blood at the gum margins. No lymphadenopathy palpable in the neck, axillae or groin. Mild splenomegaly (2 cm below the costal margin), non-tender; liver not enlarged. Chest clear, heart sounds normal with an irregularly irregular pulse. No focal neurology, no meningism, no bony tenderness of the sternum beyond mild discomfort on percussion. Right knee osteoarthritic but not inflamed. No cellulitis, no line, no catheter.
imaging: Chest radiograph clear. Abdominal ultrasound confirms mild splenomegaly (13.5 cm) with no focal lesion and normal liver; no significant lymphadenopathy.
microbiology: Blood cultures and urine culture sent as part of the pancytopenia workup and were negative at 48 hours; the patient remained afebrile without a septic focus.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute leukaemia (acute myeloid leukaemia in an older adult) — pancytopenia with circulating blasts
Marrow infiltration by other malignancy / myelodysplastic syndrome transforming
Immune thrombocytopenia (does not explain anaemia, neutropenia or blasts)
Warfarin-related bleeding / drug-induced cytopenia (excluded by circulating blasts)
finalDiagnosis: Acute leukaemia (acute myeloid leukaemia) presenting with pancytopenia and circulating myeloblasts in an elderly hospitalised patient on polypharmacy; bruising initially mis-attributed to warfarin.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Acute Myeloid Leukemia
European LeukemiaNet (ELN) — Diagnosis and Management of AML in Adults, 2022
stewardship: Non-infective presentation. No empiric antibiotics are indicated because the patient is afebrile with no septic focus, despite neutropenia. Antimicrobials should be started only if he develops fever or clinical sepsis (then treat as neutropenic fever). The immediate priority is haematology referral, transfusion support (platelets for count <20 or bleeding; red cells for symptomatic anaemia), holding warfarin given profound thrombocytopenia and reversing/bridging AF anticoagulation, and tumour-lysis prophylaxis (hydration, continue/optimise allopurinol, monitor urate/potassium/phosphate). Polypharmacy should be rationalised and renally dosed.
contraindications: Avoid intramuscular injections and non-essential invasive procedures given platelets 21 and INR 2.4
Withhold warfarin; do not continue therapeutic anticoagulation with severe thrombocytopenia
Avoid NSAIDs/antiplatelet agents that worsen bleeding risk
Do not give empiric antibiotics in the absence of fever or sepsis merely because of neutropenia
Review metformin and renally-cleared drugs before any contrast or tumour-lysis-related renal impairment
edgeCases: Bruising and bleeding wrongly attributed to warfarin, delaying recognition of leukaemia
If blasts show Auer rods with a coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, rising INR/APTT), consider acute promyelocytic leukaemia — a haematological emergency requiring urgent ATRA
Profound neutropenia raises risk of occult sepsis; a single fever spike mandates immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics
Tumour lysis can be precipitated even before chemotherapy in high-blast-burden disease
expectedMaiK: Circulating blasts on the film with pancytopenia in an elderly patient indicate acute leukaemia and cannot be explained by warfarin or polypharmacy; urgent bone marrow examination with flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular studies is required, alongside transfusion support and tumour-lysis prophylaxis.
expectedNextQuestions: Any fever, rigors or localising infection given the neutropenia?
Timeline of fatigue, bruising, night sweats and weight loss?
Any prior chemotherapy, radiotherapy, benzene exposure or antecedent blood disorder (MDS)?
Current bleeding severity and sites (gums, mucosa, urine, stool, intracranial symptoms)?
Full medication and anticoagulation review including last INR and warfarin dose?
expectedInvestigations: Peripheral blood film for blast morphology and Auer rods
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy (blast percentage >20%)
Cytogenetics and molecular studies (FLT3, NPM1, PML-RARA to exclude APL)
Coagulation screen with fibrinogen and D-dimer to exclude DIC/APL
Tumour-lysis panel: urate, potassium, phosphate, calcium, renal function, LDH

investigations: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
Tumour-lysis panel (urate, K, phosphate, calcium, renal function, LDH)

regressionAssertions: Identifies acute_leukemia as the leading diagnosis from pancytopenia with circulating blasts
Recommends urgent bone marrow examination with flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular testing
Does not attribute the bleeding/cytopenia solely to warfarin or polypharmacy
Recommends withholding warfarin and platelet transfusion for severe thrombocytopenia
Does NOT prescribe empiric antibiotics in an afebrile patient without a septic focus
Institutes tumour-lysis prophylaxis and considers APL as a coagulopathic emergency
